confirmed: Read the complete markdown, lines 1-411, including the closing references; no appendix is included. The source is the 18-page journal article, volume 5, issue 1, January-June 2024, printed pp. 17-34, by Saharat Laksanasut; received January 19, revised April 25, accepted June 12, 2024 (PDF p. 1, printed p. 17, masthead/title/byline/dates; PDF p. 18, printed p. 34, last page).

One original people experiment is reported. Despite the quasi-experimental label, the paper explicitly says group allocation was random and describes simple random allocation to AI and conventional lessons; field_rct and context_class = none are supported, and has_randomized_people_study is true (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21, Methodology and Population and Samples).

The 84 are eleventh-grade students, with 42 allocated to each group, not texts, ideas, ratings, or the target population of 16,365. The sample is from Angsilapittayakom School during the second semester of academic year 2023; Table 2 explicitly reports 42 per group for the pretest (PDF p. 5, printed p. 21, Population and Samples; PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Table 2).

Each arm received 10 lesson plans over 20 hours using five CLT stages. Group A used paid ChatGPT for outlines, revisions, and drafting; Group B had no AI-assisted tools. A specific ChatGPT model is not named (PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 21-22, Research Instruments items 1-2).

The pretest and posttest each allowed 50 minutes; posttest followed the 20-hour teaching sessions and used a different prompt. Devices and internet access were prohibited, supporting after_ai and ai_available_when_produced = no; calendar delay is not stated. Narratives typically contained 300 to 500 words (PDF pp. 7-10, printed pp. 23-26, Research Instruments item 3 and Data Collection items 2-4).

Only the 25-point creative-writing composite is reported, covering five 5-point dimensions: creativity, development, voice, literary devices, and literary conventions. No separate creativity-component or diversity result is given (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. 24-25, Table 1; PDF pp. 10-12, printed pp. 26-28, Tables 2-4).

Inter-rater Pearson correlations are 0.98 for researcher/native speaker A, 0.94 for researcher/native speaker B, and 0.97 for native speakers A/B (PDF p. 7, printed p. 23, Research Instruments item 3).

Table 2 pretest: Group A N = 42, M = 11.46, S.D. = 7.12; Group B N = 42, M = 12.86, S.D. = 8.23; t = 1.04; Sig. = 0.35; footnote says no statistical significance at a 0.01 level (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26).

Table 3 Group A before/after: M = 11.46, S.D. = 7.12 versus M = 22.72, S.D. = 5.72; t = 17.91; Sig. = 0.00*, with the asterisk denoting significance at 0.01. Data Analysis identifies this as a paired-samples t-test; Table 3 does not print N (PDF p. 11, printed p. 27).

Table 4 posttest: Group A M = 22.72, S.D. = 5.72 versus Group B M = 19.82, S.D. = 7.42; t = 14.46; Sig. = 0.00*, with the asterisk denoting significance at 0.01. These numerical results in the one-line finding match the PDF; the test is described as independent-samples, but Table 4 does not print N (PDF p. 12, printed p. 28, Table 4; PDF p. 11, printed p. 27, Data Analysis item 3).

This is not a synthesis; no pooled estimates or synthesis study counts apply. No preregistration, data/code availability statement, or supplementary-material reference is stated in the full document (PDF pp. 1-18, printed pp. 17-34).
summary: The paper reports random allocation of 84 students to ChatGPT-assisted or conventional lessons and belongs in the two-screener pipeline. The printed outcome statistics match the form, but posttest analysis counts are not explicitly reported and several descriptive claims require correction.
